response:
Formally, a problem is a binary relation between a set of possible inputs and a set of possible outputs. For each input, the relation says which outputs are correct [2][3]. You can picture it as a bipartite graph, with edges joining each input to its correct outputs [2].

An input can have more than one correct output. If the problem is "give me an index in this array that contains the value five", and five appears several times, then any of those indices is correct [2].

Specifying a problem by listing the right answer for every input ("for input one the answer is zero, for input two it's three...") would take forever, especially since 6.006 cares about arbitrarily large inputs, not small instances [1][3]. Instead we give a verifiable predicate, a property that a correct output must satisfy. Given an input and a proposed output, you can check whether the output is correct [1][3]. For the array example, you look at the index you were given and check that the value there equals five [1].

One contrast to keep in mind: a problem allows many correct outputs per input, but an algorithm is a deterministic procedure that returns a single output for each input. It solves the problem if that output is correct for every input [3][4].
reference: A problem is a binary relation from problem inputs to correct outputs. Since listing the correct output for every input would take too long, we usually give a verifiable predicate (a property) that correct outputs must satisfy.

Think about what a proof has to cover. Your code is a fixed, small number of lines, but the input can be any size: a class of 300 students, or a billion [6]. Infinitely many possible input sizes means you can't check them one by one.

Induction matches that structure. A loop or recursion is one small step repeated, and induction proves one small step and then chains it across all sizes [2]. An interface says what you want to do; a data structure says how you do it. The interface is a specification, the problem. The data structure is a representation, the solution. [1][2]

An interface is just the collection of operations that are supported (it is also called an API or ADT). For example, the Sequence interface includes operations like build(X), len(), get_at(i), set_at(i, x), insert_last(x) and delete_first(). It tells you what each operation does, but not how it is done. [1]

A data structure is the actual way the data is stored so that those operations work. Just storing data is easy, and the operations are what make it interesting. [2]

The key point is that the same interface can be implemented by many different data structures. They differ in which operations are faster, so you choose the one that suits how you will use it. [3] So you make two decisions: first that the interface is correct for the problem, then that the data structure's efficiency and memory usage match your priorities. [6]

Example: a stack is an interface that only needs insert_last(x) and delete_last(). [1] How you store the items behind it is the data structure's job.
reference: An interface (also called an API or ADT) is a specification of what operations are supported, i.e., the problem. A data structure is a representation that says how those operations are supported, i.e., the solution; different data structures can implement the same interface with different performance.

Because they are only interfaces, any data structure that supports those operations can implement them, for example a linked list or a dynamic array [6].

With 100 items that gives you room for about 100 more inserts before the next reallocation. The two algorithms work in opposite directions. Selection sort chooses the biggest item, puts it at the end, and then sorts everything to its left [3]. It keeps choosing the biggest remaining element and swapping it into the back, then repeats on what is left [6]. Insertion sort runs in the reverse order: it sorts everything to the left first, then inserts a new item into that sorted part [3].

In the notes, insertion sort recursively sorts the prefix A[:i], then sorts A[:i + 1] assuming A[:i] is already sorted, using repeated swaps [1]. So the new last element is swapped leftwards until it sits in the right place [1].

Selection sort instead starts at the back. It finds the biggest item, 9, and swaps it with the last item, 3, giving [8, 2, 4, 3, 9]. Then it finds the biggest of the rest, 8, and swaps it into the next-to-last slot, giving [3, 2, 4, 8, 9], and it continues until the front is sorted too [6].

In short, selection sort does the hard work of choosing, and the position is then fixed. Insertion sort makes the choice trivial (it just takes the next item), and the hard work is inserting it into the right spot. Both end up as order n^2 algorithms [3].
